title: Fair Witness: Insured Human Eyes for Remote Deals
one_liner: Heinlein's Fair Witnesses (professionals who report only what they observe) as a bonded, API-callable network that confirms the physical facts of remote transactions for people and buying agents.
customer: High-value peer-to-peer and consignment resellers (watches, pro camera gear, instruments, equipment), small landlords and property managers (move-in and move-out deposit disputes), insurers, and procurement teams or agents that need physical-world confirmation of goods received or site status.
problem: Remote deals stall on the physical world. Photos are easy to fake with generative editing, and signed-capture standards are not enough on their own (a researcher demonstrated forgery of C2PA credentials on Android in August 2026). Existing inspection services are siloed by category.
solution: Train and certify witnesses (retired inspectors, notaries) in a strict 'observe, do not infer' protocol. Capture happens on attested devices with a server-issued freshness challenge (a random code shown in frame, live geo and time nonce), 360-degree and macro video and calibrated measurements. Deliver a structured Witness Report (JSON plus signed media plus witness declaration) via API. Witnesses carry professional liability, and each report is insured up to a stated limit.
why_now: Generative editing has made photo evidence untrustworthy, while hardware-signed capture (Pixel 10 with C2PA) is only partly reliable. Agentic purchasing means software is becoming the buyer that needs a physical-world oracle, and no one supplies one with liability behind it.
revenue_model: $45-150 per visit, a monthly platform fee for API and marketplace integrations, and an insurance margin on the report guarantee.
non_obvious_insight: Camera signatures alone cannot carry trust. Trust is procedure plus a named person plus a liability plus freshness, which is exactly Heinlein's fair witness. Because witnesses give facts, not opinions, they are cheap to train (a few hours) and legally credible as fact witnesses. To avoid being another freelancer marketplace, staff is certified and insured, protocol-bound and sold through an API.
first_30_days: Recruit and certify 30 witnesses in one metro. Partner with two consignment resellers or a small-landlord association. Run 200 paid visits at about $60 and publish an anonymized accuracy and dispute-rate report.

title: Human Reach Audits for Newsletter and Podcast Sponsors
one_liner: Bot- and agent-scrubbed reach certificates that let honest newsletters and podcasts charge sponsors for verified human eyeballs.
customer: Newsletter and podcast operators with $5k-200k/month in sponsorship revenue on the sell side, and B2B sponsors, creator agencies and marketplaces on the buy side.
problem: Cloudflare's CEO says bots are about 20% of traffic and will exceed human traffic by 2027, with agents hitting about 1,000x more sites than a human. Opens, clicks and downloads increasingly come from scanners and AI assistants, not people. B2B sponsors buying through marketplaces such as Passionfroot and Agentio will see CPA misses and disputes, and start discounting all creators. Honest operators are hurt most.
solution: Connect to the newsletter platform and podcast host logs (Beehiiv, Ghost, Mailchimp, Libsyn, Buzzsprout). Classify every open, click and download as human, scanner or agent using timing, IP ranges, user-agent patterns and hidden honeypot links. Issue a 'Verified Human Reach' certificate with methodology and monitor it monthly, plus a sponsor-facing verify link. Later, offer pricing per verified-human click.
why_now: The bot-share trend is now being stated by infrastructure CEOs, B2B creator marketplaces are scaling (Passionfroot $15M, Agentio $40M), and reader-side detection has entered the mainstream through Substack's Pangram scan. Sponsors are getting more skeptical this budget cycle.
revenue_model: $199-499 per audit, $99/month monitoring, marketplace API fees per certificate, and a performance fee on verified-human click pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The authenticity gap that moves money is not in the content but in the audience. Sponsors buy human attention, and a certificate lets honest creators earn a premium rather than being averaged down.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 sponsor-funded newsletters via Beehiiv and Substack communities and offer a free 'what percent of your clicks are bots' scan in exchange for publishing an anonymized benchmark. Sell certificates before their next media-kit refresh, and pitch two B2B marketplaces or agencies.

title: Parametric Lease-Up Delay Insurance
one_liner: Insurance that pays automatically if a public submarket days-to-lease index stays high during a building's lease-up, protecting developers' interest carry.
customer: Multifamily developers and construction and mezzanine lenders with 100-400 unit buildings in lease-up (1.2M units nationally), sold through debt brokers.
problem: Lease-up interest carry balloons when time-to-lease stretches (34 days, longest September since 2019, with concessions on 15.8% of stabilized units). Lenders demand reserves or personal guarantees, sponsors self-insure, and traditional delay-in-start-up cover only addresses physical damage.
solution: A parametric policy that pays a pre-agreed sum if an index of median days-to-lease or vacancy exceeds a strike for N months in the lease-up window. Priced with an actuarial model, backed by reinsurer capacity, and sold as carry cover or a lender-accepted replacement for personal guarantees.
why_now: Lease-up glut and tight balance sheets create demand, parametric infrastructure (fronting carriers, index data, automated payouts) has matured, and starts are down 15.5%, so risk may be front-loaded.
revenue_model: 6-10% rate on line on $1-5M limits, plus MGA commission and profit share.
non_obvious_insight: Developers cannot influence a submarket's days-to-lease, so it is transparent and free of fraud, which makes it insurable. Capacity providers can view this as a defined macro bet with a supply-starts-driven mean reversion, though correlation across deals is the key risk.
first_30_days: Build an index from public rent and vacancy data. Quote 10 hypothetical developer and lender deals. Partner with a parametric MGA or coverholder for risk-carrying capacity and sign one $500K-limit pilot.

title: Cancellation Compliance for Regional Gym Chains
one_liner: A drop-in cancel-and-freeze portal that meets each state's auto-renewal rules and writes straight into the billing system.
customer: Regional gym and studio chains with 10-300 locations still using in-person or certified-mail cancellations, and franchisors.
problem: The FTC's national click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, but enforcement continues (the FTC sued Fitness International/LA Fitness over cancellation hurdles), state auto-renewal laws demand online cancellation if you joined online, and New York City's own click-to-cancel rule takes effect October 1, 2026. Chains run legacy contracts and billing where cancellation is manual, so exposure is AG settlements and class actions.
solution: A white-labeled 'Cancel, Pause, Downgrade' portal with a jurisdiction rules engine (notice periods, save-offer limits, refund proration, confirmations) that writes to the chain's billing platform through API or RPA, with audit logs and legally bounded retention offers.
why_now: NYC's October 1, 2026 deadline, the FTC's restart of subscription rulemaking, and active state AG scrutiny create a dated trigger with budget.
revenue_model: $150-400 per location per month plus $2k setup; share of saved revenue on approved retention flows.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance opens the door, retention pays for it: a compliant flow with legally allowed save offers often lifts net retention versus the friction chains use today, so the CFO buys it. The moat is the multi-state rules matrix plus billing-system integrations.
first_30_days: Build a rules matrix for 10 states plus NYC with a consumer-protection lawyer, sell a $1k mystery-shop 'compliance scan' of each chain's cancellation flow to 20 regional chains, and convert two into design partners.

title: Rain-Day Revenue Insurance for Patio Restaurants
one_liner: Parametric weather cover for restaurants: pick your bad-weather trigger, get paid automatically when it hits, with payouts calibrated to your own POS history.
customer: Independent restaurants and bars with 1-10 units and meaningful patio or walk-up dependence, starting in weather-volatile metros (rain, extreme heat, wildfire smoke). The owner pays a seasonal premium of roughly $40-150 per location per month. A licensed MGA/carrier partner and reinsurer sit behind the product.
problem: A rainy Friday, a 105F heat-index evening or a smoke day (AQI over 150) can cut a patio-dependent night by 30-50%. The food is already prepped and the staff are already scheduled, so almost all of the lost revenue is lost margin. Business-interruption insurance needs physical damage, so weather-driven demand loss is uninsured. Every owner knows their 'rain tax' (I know a wet Saturday costs me several thousand dollars), yet no one sells a hedge for it.
solution: Owners connect Toast, Square or Clover, and we ingest 12-24 months of hourly sales. We fit each location's loss curve against local weather-station history, for example rain over 0.15 in between 5 and 9pm Fri-Sun, or heat index above 105. The owner picks triggers and a fixed payout per trigger day. When the station data crosses the threshold, the payout goes out automatically by instant rails, with no claim and no adjuster. Because triggers are calibrated per restaurant, basis risk is low, which is what has kept carriers away from this segment. We sell it as a seasonal policy with a monthly premium.
why_now: POS APIs now give clean hourly sales for thousands of independents in minutes. Weather-station and air-quality data are cheap and auditable. Instant payment rails (FedNow, RTP) exist. Heat domes and smoke seasons are making weather volatility a top-3 owner complaint. Reinsurers are hungry for parametric programs, and restaurants face rising conventional premiums that push them to look for smarter cover. I could not re-verify current competitors this session, so check the existing parametric MGAs and event-cancellation carriers before building.
revenue_model: MGA commission plus underwriting margin on premium, typically 15-30% of premium retained as fee and MGA share. Roughly $500-1,800 per location per year in premium. Add a fee for the POS-calibrated loss-curve analytics, sold to carriers and reinsurers as a data product.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is that the owner's POS data, not a claims adjuster, is the underwriting. Basis risk is what kills parametric for small businesses, and a restaurant's own hourly sales history fixes it. Insurers think restaurants are too heterogeneous to price. They are only heterogeneous until you fit each one separately. The loss is also asymmetric: prepped food and committed labor mean a payout only has to cover the lost contribution margin, not the revenue, so premiums can be low.
first_30_days: Use my two locations' POS exports plus 10 friendly patio owners' data to fit loss curves and prove the weather-to-sales correlation. Publish a free 'Rain Tax Report' for one metro to generate leads. Sign a licensed MGA or fronting-carrier partner. Collect 10-15 signed letters of intent at about $60 per month for the next patio season. Since it is late September, use the off-season to finish modeling and pre-sell spring renewals.

title: N-of-1 Trial Network for the Peptide Boom
one_liner: IRB-supervised, blinded, randomized N-of-1 trials that let peptide users learn what works for them while building the missing evidence base.
customer: Consumers already using or considering BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu or KPV (pay ~$249 per 12-week trial), plus clinics, 503A pharmacies, wearable and supplement brands that need substantiation.
problem: Peptides are legal-ish again (HHS Feb 2026; FDA panel Jul 23, 2026 backed BPC-157 and KPV despite agency concerns), yet there is no evidence base. Users self-experiment uncontrolled, clinics cannot substantiate claims, and the FDA panel itself flagged the gaps.
solution: A 503A pharmacy ships coded vials (active vs placebo, randomized crossover), an app collects pre-registered endpoints (pain scores, sleep, grip strength, wearable HRV) plus baseline and 8-week safety labs, and Bayesian analysis returns each person's answer and contributes to a public aggregated dataset. Start with BPC-157 for tendon and joint pain.
why_now: Peptide deregulation in 2026, cheap wearables and remote endpoints, AI-assisted protocol design and statistics, and a crowd of volunteers already injecting. N-of-1 designs need tens of people per question, not hundreds.
revenue_model: $249 per participant, $50-150k sponsor-funded studies from clinics and brands, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: When regulation retreats, credible evidence becomes the scarce good. The crowd already volunteers, and pre-registered N-of-1 series can outrun a traditional RCT for low-risk, subjective-endpoint questions.
first_30_days: Draft protocol and IRB submission with an FDA IND-exemption determination from counsel. Recruit ~60 people through biohacker communities and one partner clinic. Line up a 503A pharmacy for blinded placebo and open a $249 waitlist for the first cohort.

title: Random-Sample CPA Audits of AI Bookkeeping
one_liner: A $79/month independent assurance layer where a licensed CPA reviews a random sample of a micro-business's AI-categorized transactions and signs a monthly accuracy attestation backed by a penalty-reimbursement guarantee.
customer: Nonemployers and 1-10 employee businesses (contractors, salons, restaurants, e-commerce sellers) using AI bookkeeping in QuickBooks, Xero or startup tools. Secondary buyers are AI-bookkeeping vendors wanting white-label certification and lenders wanting attested books.
problem: 46% of AI-using small firms name accuracy as their top problem (Fed SBCS 2026). Intuit and Xero are pushing LLM categorization to millions of users, and Bench's Dec 2024 collapse locked customers out of their books for days. Owners find errors only at a tax bill, a loan denial or a penalty, and new OBBBA reporting (tips and overtime, the $2,000 1099 floor) raises the cost of misclassification.
solution: Stratified sampling weighted toward high-dollar, first-seen-vendor and deduction-sensitive transactions. The CPA confirms against receipts and bank data, fixes errors inside the customer's own software, and issues a monthly signed 'books verified' report with a measured error rate. A small reserve (later insurer-backed) reimburses penalties traceable to verified periods. Every attestation exports to a portable audit file that survives any vendor failing.
why_now: Mass-market LLM bookkeeping arrived in 2026 (Intuit-Anthropic and Xero-Anthropic partnerships) just as CPA headcount stalled near 678K. Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices, which signals that pure-AI trust is unsolved. No incumbent can credibly sell independent assurance on its own output.
revenue_model: $79/month per business with reviewer cost of roughly $15-25/month after AI triage. Add $2-5K/year white-label fees from AI bookkeepers, lender attestation fees, and warranty margin once insurer-backed.
non_obvious_insight: Checking is roughly ten times cheaper than doing, so scarce CPAs can serve 10x more clients as auditors of samples than as preparers. Auditors must be independent of the producer, a position structurally closed to Intuit and Xero. The accumulated error-rate data by tool becomes a Consumer Reports-style asset that the vendors cannot publish themselves.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired CPAs and sign 20 founding clients at $49 from contractor and salon-owner communities. Run a blind test of three AI bookkeepers on 50 anonymized sets of books and publish the error rates for press. Pitch 3 small bookkeeping firms to resell the attestation.

title: Tariff Refund Rescue for Micro-Importers
one_liner: A flat-fee triage, protest and pooled-filing service that recovers IEEPA tariff refunds for small importers whose entries fell outside the automated CBP refund system.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $5K-$250K of IEEPA duties paid: direct-import Shopify/Amazon/Etsy sellers, small distributors, restaurants and retailers who imported containers. Not the big players, who already have trade lawyers. They pay a flat audit fee plus a success fee on money recovered. Lenders and claim buyers are a secondary customer.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP's CAPE refund portal opened Apr 20 and initially covered only about 63% of entries. Entries that were finally liquidated, are under protest, or have mixed statuses fall outside it. The 180-day protest clock runs per entry. Trade lawyers quote $10,000-$15,000, which wipes out a $15,000 refund. Small importers hold these stuck entries and cannot justify the fees, while interest accrues at 6%.
solution: Software plus a small ops desk. The importer uploads ACE reports or grants read-only ACE access. The tool sorts every entry into CAPE-eligible, protest window still open (with a per-entry deadline calendar), or finally liquidated. It auto-builds CAPE declarations for self-filers, protest packets, and a standardized pooled Court of International Trade joinder or complaint filed by a partner trade law firm at a flat per-importer price. It also verifies and bundles small claims into $20M+ pools that lenders and claim buyers will finance. That gives importers cash now instead of a 60-90+ day wait. Non-lawyers cannot share legal fees, so the legal work is a separate flat fee to partner counsel.
why_now: CAPE Phase 1 opened Apr 20, 2026 and Phase 2 on Jun 29. The CIT issued reliquidation orders for finally liquidated entries on Jul 15 and Jul 21, but it is unclear whether non-litigants must sue. In late September 2026, coverage says refunds remain 'caught between Customs and the courts'. Protest windows on spring-2026 liquidations are expiring right now. The Feb-Sept 2026 window will not repeat.
revenue_model: $99-$299 triage fee, credited toward a 7-12% success fee on refunds recovered (software and ops, not legal fees). A flat pass-through fee to partner counsel for CIT filings. Portfolio-packaging fee, paid by the lender or claim buyer, on pooled small claims that meet institutional minimums.
non_obvious_insight: The money is in the long tail, not the big importers. The US Chamber says 300,000+ companies and about $166B in duties are affected, across 53M+ entries (https://www.uschamber.com/economy/tariff-refunds-faq-what-small-businesses-need-to-know-after-supreme-courts-ruling). A Sept 2026 report says small importers are stuck because $10K-$15K legal costs can exceed the refund itself, and that importers have entries spread across unliquidated, protest-window and final statuses at the same time (https://kvia.com/stacker-international/2026/09/22/months-after-ieepa-tariffs-were-struck-down-some-refunds-remain-caught-between-customs-and-the-courts/). Meanwhile the refund-claims secondary market is estimated at up to $100B, trading at up to 60 cents on the dollar, but lenders want a minimum $10M loan against at least $20M of claims (https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/04/ieepa-tariff-refund-claims-key-considerations-for-lenders-borrowers-and-claims-purchasers). Nobody aggregates the small claims. The wedge is a per-entry deadline calendar and standardized filing packet, plus pooling for liquidity, not legal advice.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build an ACE-report parser that outputs entry buckets and protest deadlines, and sign a flat-fee arrangement with a licensed customs broker and a CIT-admitted trade attorney. Days 8-20: post the free 'which of my entries are stuck?' triage tool in small-importer communities (Shopify and Amazon private-label groups, freight forwarder mailing lists, Reddit r/importing). Target 30 uploads. Days 21-30: convert 8-10 importers to paid protest or pooled filings, and record the recovered dollars as case studies for the lender pooling pitch.

title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Dead Importers
one_liner: A contingency service that finds failed or dormant importers whose IEEPA refund claims are stranded, revives them or works through their bankruptcy trustee, and files the claims through a licensed broker.
customer: Chapter 7 trustees and ABC assignees of failed importers, plus founders of dissolved or dormant small importers. They pay 20-30% of recovered dollars. Secondary customers are claim buyers who want vetted entry-level claim files.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP is now refunding through CAPE in phases: Phase 1 opened Apr 20 for unliquidated and recently liquidated entries, Phase 2 came in June, and Phase 3 (late July) covers finally liquidated entries only for importers who sued at the CIT. Refunds go to the importer of record (or the broker who filed the entry). Every entry has its own clock, including the 180-day protest window. A large tail of small importers closed or went dark during the 2025 tariff shock. Their refunds are six-figure receivables spread across hundreds of ACE entries. They appear on nobody's balance sheet, and nobody at the dead company is watching for them. A trustee liquidating the estate usually does not know the asset exists.
solution: Build an entry-level refund estimator from public bill-of-lading data, HTS lines, country of origin and the IEEPA rate schedule. Cross-match importer names against state dissolution lists and PACER filings to rank stranded claims by likely dollar value. Then run the recovery: (1) approach trustees with an asset-discovery letter and a court-approvable contingency engagement; (2) for dissolved entities, reinstate the corporation under state law, re-enroll ACH, and file CF-4811 designations where needed; (3) have a licensed broker file CAPE declarations for the entries that broker filed; (4) send finally liquidated entries to partner trade counsel for CIT reliquidation orders under the July 17 order. The moat is a licensed-broker partner plus a pipeline of claims that nobody else is hunting.
why_now: IEEPA was struck down Feb 20, 2026. CAPE phases rolled out Apr-Jul 2026, and the July 17 CIT order created a court-driven Phase 3. Per-entry deadlines are now running. Existing refund tools (deadline trackers and CAPE filing helpers) all sell to living importers who are already paying attention. Nobody productized the orphaned-claim hunt.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on refunds recovered, plus interest. Trustee engagements are approved by the bankruptcy court as contingency fee arrangements. A secondary line sells diligenced claim packages to claim buyers at a flat fee per package.
non_obvious_insight: The refund is attached to the importer-of-record number, not to whoever was actually hurt, and only the IOR or the filing broker can claim it in the early phases. Brokers hold the entry data but their powers of attorney die with the client, and chasing a dead client is unbillable work, so nobody does it. A broker can still file CAPE for entries it filed, which makes the broker the key that unlocks these claims. Outsiders see the refund as a tax-accounting topic. Insiders see it as an unclaimed-property hunt across ACE.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 2025 importer-level volumes for China, Vietnam, India and other tariffed origins from ImportYeti or a cheap paid BOL feed, then estimate each importer's IEEPA duty. Week 2: cross-match against CA, NY, TX, FL and NJ dissolution records and PACER chapter 7 and ABC filings, and rank the top 150 targets above about $50k. Week 3: send trustees a one-page asset-discovery letter, since trustee contact info is public, and have a trade lawyer draft the contingency engagement. Week 4: sign the first 3-5 estates, or dormant founders, and file the first CAPE declarations through the partner broker.

title: Zero-Commission Motor Third-Party Renewal Rails
one_liner: If motor third-party pays agents 0%, nobody sells the mandatory cover, so insurers need a cost-plus renewal utility.
customer: Indian general insurers, especially public-sector ones, and fleet owners; insurers pay a per-renewal fee.
problem: The IRDAI draft (Sep 23) cuts commission caps from 30% to 20%, sets 0% on motor third-party and 5% on own-damage. PB Fintech fell 36% in a day, and agents and aggregators lose any reason to chase mandatory renewals.
solution: Automated renewal reminders using expiry data from dealers and registration records, sent as WhatsApp messages in local languages with UPI payment. Charge a flat servicing fee. The wedge is two-wheeler third-party renewals in one state for one insurer.
why_now: The draft is out for comment now, and insurers must find distribution that costs less than commission.
revenue_model: Rs 30-80 per renewal from the insurer, with own-damage upsell.
non_obvious_insight: When distribution stops paying, a mandatory product needs a utility rather than a marketplace, and the underwriter is the natural buyer. The draft could change, so build for both outcomes.
first_30_days: Pitch three insurers. Run a 5,000-vehicle renewal test using expiry lists from a dealer network.

title: Water Due Diligence for Senior Housing Deals
one_liner: A 'Phase I for water' that grades a senior living property or CCRC bond on supply security, drought exposure, contamination compliance and in-building Legionella risk before lenders and buyers commit.
customer: HUD-232 and bridge lenders, senior-housing acquirers and Sunbelt developers, CCRC bond underwriters and muni credit analysts, and insurers. Pricing is $4-12k per deal report and $25-60k a year for portfolio subscriptions.
problem: Senior housing occupancy is 90.1%, the highest since 2007, and construction is the lowest since 2012 with a roughly $275B shortfall. New development will restart in Sunbelt states where Colorado River cuts (2027+), groundwater rules, PFAS and lead compliance, and drought restrictions bite. The asset class is uniquely exposed: 24/7 occupancy, heavy laundry, kitchens and cooling towers, frail residents you cannot evacuate, and Legionella that kills mostly older adults. CCRC bonds promise care for life on 30-year horizons, yet a standard environmental Phase I says nothing about water security.
solution: A standard report covering legally deliverable supply, the provider's source portfolio (river, groundwater, reuse), moratorium and curtailment history, a five-year rate outlook, PFAS, lead and nitrate compliance of the serving utility, and an in-building water-management-plan audit (Legionella per CMS and ASHRAE 188, cooling towers). It also covers drought-restriction impacts on operations and NOI sensitivity to a 30% water-cost spike. Output is a letter grade plus capex and insurance recommendations, with a portfolio dashboard for bond analysts.
why_now: Record occupancy and accelerating investment mean a wave of acquisitions and new starts is coming. The Colorado River decision framework landed in Aug 2026, PFAS monitoring starts in 2027, and Texas's data-center water crackdown showed water is now an explicit siting factor.
revenue_model: Per-report fees of $4-12k, annual subscriptions of $25-60k for bond funds and lender credit desks, and remediation referral fees from the sensor and water-treatment vendors that fix the flagged items.
non_obvious_insight: For senior housing, water risk is life-safety, not just cost. Residents cannot leave and the pathogens are lethal, so it should be underwritten like fire risk, yet nobody sells the underwriting standard. The first credible grade becomes the lender checklist item.
first_30_days: Publish a free water-risk map of the 60 largest CCRC and senior-housing bond issuers in Colorado River, Texas and Florida stress zones. Email it to 30 muni analysts and 10 HUD lenders, and offer three discounted deal reports at $3k.

title: A Suable LLC With Reserves for Every Agent
one_liner: Mass-produced, series-LLC legal wrappers that give each paid agent a registered agent for service of process, a capital reserve, and tax handling, so counterparties have someone to sue.
customer: Indie developers and small studios monetizing paid agents, MCP servers and pay-per-call endpoints (they pay). Enterprise buyers and buying agents use the registry for free. Later, enterprises that want internal agents to contract externally without exposing the parent company.
problem: An agent cannot be sued, hold a bank account or be a contract party. A buyer's counsel asks 'who is my counterparty?' and the honest answer is a 22-year-old with a Discord handle. Sellers, meanwhile, face personal liability and VAT/sales-tax obligations across dozens of jurisdictions from micro-sales made without any human checkout.
solution: One low-cost Delaware or Wyoming series-LLC cell per agent, created in batch: registered agent, EIN, bank or stablecoin account, and a mandatory reserve (say $500-5,000) held in T-bills. The agent's public key is registered so any counterparty can resolve key to entity to reserve balance to claims history. Buying agents can enforce a rule such as 'reserve at least 20x order size'. An embedded merchant-of-record partner handles VAT and sales tax, and an optional insurance rider covers errors.
why_now: x402-style stablecoin micro-payments let agents sell without any human checkout. Legal commentators in 2026 are publishing playbooks for wrapping autonomous agents in LLCs (for example Aaron Wright's essay on the agent's legal body and Ledger's work on registered AI entities). Regimes such as California's have made 'the AI did it' no defense, so buyers now want a named responsible entity.
revenue_model: $49 per agent per month plus $99 formation fee, yield on pooled reserves (roughly 4% on float), 1% merchant-of-record fee, and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Identity is the wrong primitive. Strangers trust each other when the counterparty has something to lose and somewhere a summons can be served, which is exactly what corporations were invented to provide. The reserve is the product and the reputation score is a byproduct. Caveat: veil-piercing and principal liability still apply, so the product must be candid that it makes agents serviceable and collateralized, not judgment-proof.
first_30_days: Partner with a registered-agent firm and one series-LLC attorney. Offer 50 founding 'agent cells' to MCP and paid-endpoint developers via developer communities and X. Handle paperwork in manual batches. Validate demand by getting two enterprise buyers to say they will only purchase from agents with a registered entity and reserve.

title: Surety-Bonded License Plates for AI Agents
one_liner: A registrar that binds each autonomous agent to a legally accountable, insured principal through a surety bond and a revocable credential merchants and platforms can check.
customer: Agent developers and vendors that need acceptance by merchants, booking and B2B procurement platforms, the merchants and platforms that want to admit agents safely, and surety insurers or MGAs.
problem: Visa, Mastercard and Amex are activating agent payments in 2026, but dispute and liability infrastructure barely exists. Merchants bear the chargebacks, and Mastercard is reportedly planning scheme-carried liability for certified agents. Identity schemes such as Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Cloudflare's signed agents say who an agent is, but not who pays when it misbehaves.
solution: Register the agent and underwrite it with a test suite, spend caps and a behaviour policy. Issue a signed credential with a visible bond limit, and let merchants and platforms verify it with one API call. A claims process pays merchants for agent-caused losses, and violations revoke the credential. Start with an MGA and fronting-carrier partnership.
why_now: Card networks are moving on agent payments in 2026, Lloyd's-backed AI liability covers launched in 2025, and merchants are asking who is liable for agent orders. Signed-agent identity standards exist, so the missing layer is accountability.
revenue_model: Annual premium of 1-5% of bond limit, a registration fee, and float on the claims reserve.
non_obvious_insight: Identity without liability is theatre. The mature trust machine for strangers who might not pay is suretyship (contractor licences, notary bonds), not a reputation score, and a bond turns 'trust me' into a price.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical (restaurant and hotel booking, or B2B procurement agents). Sign five agent developers, secure a letter of intent from a surety or MGA, build the underwriting test suite, and get three merchants to trial a bonded-only allowlist.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

title: Manufactured-Home Replacement With Salvage Financing
one_liner: A turnkey 'old home out, new home in' program for manufactured-home communities: hazmat survey, salvage and teardown of pre-1976 units, pad prep, then set-and-hookup crews for new factory-built homes, with scrap and reuse value helping finance the job.
customer: Manufactured-home community owners and resident-owned communities replacing derelict units, state and nonprofit replacement programs, and chattel lenders.
problem: Old manufactured homes are a huge stock of unsubsidized affordable housing, but many are at end of life. Removing one costs thousands (asbestos survey, hazmat, disposal) and takes weeks. Even as factory-built homes get cheaper, foundations, utility hookups, set crews and local financing stay local and human. The July 2026 ROAD to Housing Act killed the steel chassis rule (about $10K or 10% of unit cost), but HUD has yet to publish the new standards.
solution: A fixed-price 'decommission and pad-ready in 10 days' package: survey, harvest steel frame, axles, aluminum, copper and appliances, and route scrap and hazmat properly. Then a set-and-hookup crew for the new home, plus a lender referral and a trade-in credit that offsets the down payment. Park owners buy the program to upgrade lots.
why_now: ROAD to Housing Act (Jul 11, 2026) makes factory-built housing cheaper and HUD's standards are imminent. Tariffs raise steel and material costs, site-crew scarcity is acute, and PE-owned parks want faster unit turnover.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of roughly $6-12K per replacement (salvage revenue offsets perhaps a fifth to a third of removal cost); lender and dealer referral fees; set-crew margin later.
non_obvious_insight: The replacement bottleneck is not the factory but the exit of the old unit. Salvage and hazmat know-how turn a cost into a program, and a trade-in credit is what makes chattel financing pencil for the resident.
first_30_days: Approach 5 park owners or resident-owned co-ops with 5-20 derelict homes each. Price a pilot batch of 10 homes. Run asbestos surveys, take scrap to yards and document real per-home cost and cycle time. Use the results to sign the first paid batch and a lender partner.

title: GLP-1 Menu Labeling Layer for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A cheap per-dish protein, fiber and portion labeling and half-portion pricing tool that tells the 12% of diners on GLP-1 drugs which dishes fit, published wherever they look.
customer: Owner-operated independent restaurants and small groups (2-30 locations), plus campus and hospital cafeterias, that sell through delivery apps and Google Maps. They pay $199 setup and $39/month.
problem: About 11-12% of US adults now take GLP-1 drugs, up from 3% in 2024 (KFF poll). Chains have reacted with lighter-portion sections, protein menus and dedicated GLP-1 menus (Olive Garden, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Subway, Smoothie King). Independents have no dietitian, no nutrition data and no way to show which dishes fit. Their menus say nothing about protein grams or half sizes, and independents are exempt from chain menu-labeling rules.
solution: The owner uploads a menu PDF or photo. The tool estimates per-dish calories, protein and fiber as a range, using LLM recipe parsing plus USDA FoodData Central. It tags dishes 'protein-first' or 'light plate' using explicit, published thresholds. It suggests a half-portion or 'box half before it reaches the table' price point that keeps margin (food cost is typically about 30% of price, so a half portion at 65-70% of price holds gross profit). It then auto-publishes to the Google Business Profile menu, DoorDash and Uber Eats descriptions, a QR menu and printable table tents, with a short staff script. All output is worded as an estimate with no medical claims.
why_now: Health-topic search data shows GLP1 at 1.5M monthly searches (+1,011%) and Fibremaxxing +7,900%, and Google's Summergeist report shows fibermaxxing at an all-time high. Chains are now marketing to this group in 2026, so independents are losing a segment that dines out often.
revenue_model: $199 setup, $39/month per location for menu updates, delivery-app syncing and 'reorder tag' analytics. Add-ons: $99 printed table tents and $149 chef-recipe reformulation consult. Later: bundle through POS resellers, delivery-marketing agencies and restaurant associations.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is communication, not the menu. A 2026 survey cited by ABC News found 89% of GLP-1 users wish restaurants 'communicated better about options that promote health and wellness' while 90% say restaurants typically do offer healthy items. The same coverage cites a National Restaurant Association survey that GLP-1 users make 7.6 restaurant purchases a week versus 5.1 for non-users. They want 'half-sized and lunch-sized portions, protein-first options... the ability to box food before it reaches the table' (https://abcnews.com/US/weight-loss-drug-usage-grows-restaurants-offer-glp/story?id=135711648). So the cheapest fix is labeling and relabeling what a kitchen already makes, not building new dishes, and nutrition-lab analysis is unnecessary. Chain moves are documented at https://www.foodingredientsfirst.com/news/glp-1-friendly-menus-food-dining-2026.html and https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/smaller-portions-protein-glp-1s-are-quietly-changing-chain-restaurant-rcna254178, which both say nothing about independents, so that segment is unserved. Search demand: https://explodingtopics.com/health-topics.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the menu parser, estimates and tag thresholds, and have a registered dietitian review the method and disclaimers. Days 8-20: walk into 30 independent restaurants in one dense neighborhood with a free 'GLP-1 menu scorecard' on their own menu, and pitch via the local restaurant association and Toast/Square consultants. Days 21-30: onboard 8-10 paying restaurants, publish updated Google Business Profile and delivery listings, and track half-portion attach rate and new-visitor searches for a case study.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Public Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee audit that finds 'tariff surcharge' line items on city, school-district, transit and university purchase orders and recovers the share vendors are now being refunded after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
customer: County and city finance departments, school districts, transit agencies, public universities and public hospitals. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered and nothing upfront.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. Roughly 330,000 importers paid about $166B, and as of July only about $86B had been repaid, so about $80B remained outstanding. Refunds go to the importer of record, not to the public buyers who paid vendor surcharges (one machine-shop supplier surcharge was 2.7%). Small importers and delivered-duty-unpaid shipments, including many university and hospital equipment imports, are likely to go unclaimed. Brokers are paid per entry and have no reason to chase this.
solution: Step 1: mine open-checkbook portals to rank vendors in tariff-exposed categories (school buses, HVAC, lab equipment, IT, furniture, playgrounds) and file public-records requests for their invoices to find surcharge lines. Step 2: send standardized pass-through refund claims and negotiate credit memos where the contract or surcharge language supports it. Step 3: where the public entity was itself importer of record (DDU), file its own refund claims. A dashboard tracks vendor refund status and the client's recovered dollars.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with liquidated-entry and AD/CVD cases coming later, so vendor cash is fresh but memory of surcharges will fade. Claim deadlines and statutes of limitation close within 12-18 months. Public entities are under budget pressure and readily accept no-cost recovery audits, as with utility-bill and sales-tax audits.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a lower fee on refunds recovered by filing as importer of record. The same platform later runs recurring price-escalation monitoring for a subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The money sits with a party who has no incentive to hand it over, while the party who bore the cost has unusual leverage: public buyers can demand transparency, make supplier performance part of the record, and threaten future award eligibility. Public procurement contracts and open-checkbook data make targets findable without any client cooperation.
first_30_days: Pull open-checkbook data for 3 states, file about 30 public-records requests for surcharge invoices, and have counsel review a standard claim letter. Cold-email 20 finance directors with a personalized 'you likely overpaid $X to Vendor Y' one-pager and sign two pilots on contingency.

title: Status-Cliff Benefit Sold Through PEOs
one_liner: A confidential, employer-paid benefit that screens temporary-status workers for alternate immigration relief, tracks work-authorization cliffs, and pre-arranges counsel and family plans before a raid, TPS termination or EAD lapse hits.
customer: Payroll, PEO and staffing firms serving labor-intensive employers (home health, poultry and meat processing, hospitality, warehousing, construction, agriculture), plus the employers themselves. They pay $4-9 per employee per month or $60-120 per screened worker.
problem: Employers with workers on TPS, humanitarian parole, pending asylum EADs or DACA are losing headcount unpredictably. Terminations of TPS and parole programs hit hundreds of thousands of workers with little warning, and automatic EAD extensions ended for renewals filed after late October 2025, so employees now fall out of I-9 validity while renewals are pending. Worksite enforcement and I-9 Notices of Inspection (3 business days to respond) are rising. HR treats it as a compliance chore, then loses 10-30% of a shift overnight.
solution: A benefit package in four parts. (1) A dashboard that projects the work-authorization cliff by employee category and date, with I-9 reverification scripts that avoid discriminatory over-documentation. (2) Confidential relief screening done by a licensed partner attorney for each willing employee (family petitions, pending asylum, U/T visas, SIJS, cancellation, adjustment eligibility) with the employee, not the employer, as the client. (3) An emergency file for each participating worker: signed G-28 on file, memorized A-number card, standby guardianship documents for children, and a hotline for the first 72 hours after a detention. (4) An I-9 pre-audit and a 72-hour Notice of Inspection response playbook.
why_now: TPS and parole terminations, the end of EAD automatic extensions, expanded enforcement, and increased I-9 audits all converged in late 2025 through 2026. Employers can no longer treat immigration compliance as an annual checkbox, and existing I-9 software only tracks expiry dates. It offers no relief screening, no emergency response, and no employee-side counsel.
revenue_model: Per-employee-per-month benefit fee split between the platform and partner law firms (structured as payment to the firm for services rendered, with the third-party-payor consent required by the professional conduct rules), plus per-screening fees and a premium I-9 audit-defense add-on. PEOs and payroll firms get a distribution margin.
non_obvious_insight: The employer's real loss is churn, not fines. In screenings, a surprisingly large share of workers, often a quarter or more in my experience, have a path they never knew about, because no one ever asked in a confidential setting. A worker who is told they have a path stays loyal to the employer that offered it. The right buyer is the PEO's benefits desk, since PEOs already sell legal-plan and EAP riders through one procurement decision.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical (home health agencies, where TPS and parole terminations are hitting staffing hardest) and one state. Partner with 2 immigration firms that have screening capacity. Pitch 3 regional agencies and 1 PEO with a 60-day pilot: 100 employees screened for $6,000, delivered as a de-identified summary of how many have alternate paths. Use the pilot data (headcount saved, cases opened) as the sales deck for the PEO channel.

title: Preflight Lab for Steam Frame Verified
one_liner: A shared hardware lab that runs your build on real Steam Frame, Steam Machine and Deck units, finds why it would fail Valve's compatibility review, and fixes it.
customer: Back-catalog publishers with 20-200 older titles, and mid-size indie studios that want the 'Great on Frame' or Steam Machine badge. They pay $250-1,500 per title for preflight plus fix, or $1-3k a month for catalog coverage.
problem: The Steam Frame is an ARM device that runs x86 games through FEX and Proton, and it launched in mid-September 2026. Only about 131 titles were Verified at launch out of tens of thousands. Valve's review is a queue with terse pass/fail notes, and each resubmission costs weeks. Failures are usually boring: launcher windows, first-run dialogs, 32-bit dependencies, cutscene codecs, kernel anti-cheat, controller glyphs, unreadable text, missing the 30fps at 720p floor. Devs can't justify buying a $1,059 headset to test.
solution: A rack of real devices with an automated runner. It launches the build through Steam, drives it with synthetic controller input, and records frame-times. It OCRs UI text height, uses a vision model to catch launcher and dialog windows, and checks the checklist Valve publishes. The output is a ranked punch-list. A paid fix-it tier handles launch options, Steam Input configs, codec swaps and small patches, then resubmits to Valve.
why_now: Steam Machine (June 29, 2026) and Steam Frame (September 2026) just shipped, with FEX and the verified-badge process brand new. The first 6-12 months of a new Valve platform are when badges are scarce and the store gives them the most weight, as happened with Deck Verified in 2022. Back-catalog publishers will want to opt in whole catalogs at once.
revenue_model: Per-title preflight and fix fees, catalog subscriptions for publishers, and a success-based 'Verified or partial refund' premium tier.
non_obvious_insight: The failures repeat across titles, so a publisher with 60 games amortizes every fix, and a lab that has fixed one FMV codec problem fixes it for a hundred games. Studios also can't afford the hardware, so shared capex becomes their opex. Triage by expected Frame-owner overlap, because the badge only pays off in genres that owners actually buy.
first_30_days: Buy 2 Frames, 1 Machine and 1 Deck (about $3.5-4k). Run 10 free preflights for devs recruited from Steam Frame and Deck communities and Linux gaming press. Publish 'the top 10 reasons Frame review fails', drawn from those real runs. Pitch 5 ports and back-catalog publishers a fixed price per title for a 20-title pilot.

title: Buyout Bridge for Flood-Prone Counties
one_liner: Run the paperwork of county flood buyouts and front cash to owners, reimbursed when grants land.
customer: County and municipal floodplain managers and state hazard-mitigation offices, paying from program administration budgets. Later, impact and philanthropic capital for the bridge fund.
problem: Risk Rating 2.0 pushes premiums toward full risk (median $689 versus about $1,288 needed, per CRS, secondary source), eroding equity in repeatedly flooded homes. Owners want out, but FEMA programs are erratic: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order and reinstated Mar 18 2026, with applications closed July 23 2026. Buyouts take years, so owners sit in limbo or sell at fire-sale prices.
solution: An operations and software backbone for county acquisition programs: eligibility, duplication-of-benefits tracking, appraisal, title, relocation counseling, demolition procurement, open-space deed restrictions and reimbursement compliance. Then add a pooled bridge fund that pays owners in 60-90 days and is repaid from grants.
why_now: The NFIP glide path to full-risk pricing, plus the BRIC cancel-and-restore whiplash, leaves states building their own programs.
revenue_model: $3-8K fixed admin fee per acquisition, and later a bridge-loan spread.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not money but cash timing and paperwork, and governments will pay for throughput more readily than for software.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with repetitive-loss acquisition backlogs and offer to run 20 properties under a $25K pilot. Publish time-to-close as the benchmark.

title: Escrowed Group Orders for Fandom Imports
one_liner: A group-order platform for K-pop, anime and idol merchandise that escrows money, consolidates freight under formal customs entry, and splits domestic shipping.
customer: Group-order managers (volunteer fans running orders on X, Instagram and Discord) and the fans who join their orders, plus small importers.
problem: US de minimis ended on 29 Aug 2025, so single parcels from Korea can be dutiable. Group orders run on PayPal Friends and Family and trust, and fraud is rife: Korea's police reported foreign-national fraud complaints rising from 5,307 (2023) to 19,907 (2025). Group-order managers personally carry the customs and refund risk.
solution: Managers list an order, participants pay into escrow, we purchase against verified receipts and aggregate into one commercial shipment (broker-filed entry, duties and product-safety rules handled), then split to US addresses with tracking. A reputation score for managers and automatic refunds when an order fails.
why_now: The de minimis change turned informal parcel-splitting into an importer-of-record problem, and scam volume is surging.
revenue_model: A 4-6% escrow fee, a freight and handling margin, and a manager subscription for tools.
non_obvious_insight: The informal fan trust economy has no importer and no escrow. Whoever becomes the compliant importer of record plus payment escrow captures the volume, because managers cannot solve duty on their own.
first_30_days: Partner with 5 mid-size US group-order managers. Run 3 orders end to end through a Korean freight forwarder. Charge the escrow fee and publish a public scam tracker for credibility.

title: Community Radio as a Paid Knowledge API
one_liner: Turn African community-radio call-in shows into a live, district-level, per-call-priced local-truth feed that farm agents and lenders pay for, with stations keeping most of the revenue.
customer: Agri-input distributors, crop insurers, agri-lenders and farmer-facing AI agents (FarmerChat-style services) in East Africa. Community radio stations in Uganda and Kenya are the supply side and get 70% of revenue.
problem: Western models 'fail spectacularly' on African crops, and satellites cannot see this week's pest outbreak, local planting window or market price. Community radio is where farmers self-report and where trusted extension voices answer, but its ad revenue is collapsing. Bots do not click ads, so stations earn nothing when agents consume their knowledge.
solution: Transcribe and structure weekly call-in shows (Luganda, Swahili, Hausa and others) into dated, sourced, district-level signals such as pest reports, price quotes and planting advice, with provenance and consent. Expose them as an MCP or HTTP endpoint with per-call micropayments via x402 or MPP. Add a paid 'ask the station' tier where an agent's question is read on air and the answer captured. Stations receive rev-share via mobile money.
why_now: Small ASR models (300M-1.7B parameters) now handle local languages, and AethexAI already trains on radio audio. FarmerChat has answered 8M+ questions, which proves demand. Machine-payment protocols make micro-charging per call possible, and Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl is training content owners to charge bots.
revenue_model: Per-call fees for agents ($0.005-0.05), district-level monthly subscriptions ($200-600) for lenders and insurers, and premium on-air Q&A. Platform keeps 30% and stations get 70%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a language training set, which is a commodity. It is fresh local ground truth with a trusted human voice behind it, delivered as a live feed rather than an archive. Radio stations are the last network where farmers report in their own words. Content owners who cannot win the ad economy can win the agent-query economy.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 stations in Uganda and Kenya with a simple rev-share and consent agreement. Record and transcribe two weeks of shows with a fine-tuned open ASR model. Publish a weekly district JSON feed. Sell the first two district subscriptions to an agri-lender or seed distributor at $300-500 a month.

title: Certified Scrap Kill for Aircraft Parts
one_liner: A mobile crew and app that destroys, photographs and certifies scrapped aircraft parts so they can never resurface as fake 'serviceable' parts, and sells the segregated metal.
customer: Regional airline stores and quality departments, Part 145 repair stations, lessors managing teardowns and part-outs, and engine and component shops. They pay a per-event fee, partly offset by a share of the alloy value.
problem: Every airline is supposed to mutilate parts that are beyond economical repair or time-expired so they cannot re-enter the supply chain. On the floor, the scrap cage gets emptied by a metals dealer on a handshake. Serial plates are sometimes cut off and sometimes not. Techs and stores people know that 'scrapped' units can turn up months later 'overhauled' at a broker with a tidy set of documents. The airline also carries the paper trail risk. If a fake part traces back to your serial number, you are in the investigation. Meanwhile titanium and nickel-alloy scrap is sold mixed at a low commodity price, because nobody segregates it.
solution: A van with a shear or plasma cutter, a tag punch and a phone app. Per drum or per pallet, the crew scans and photographs part number and serial number before destruction, destroys the part in a way that defeats reuse, photographs it again after, and pushes a hash-stamped certificate of destruction into the customer's inventory system. This removes the item from their books and gives quality staff and lessor auditors an unbroken chain of custody. Scrap is segregated by alloy and sold to specialty metal buyers, which funds the service.
why_now: Scrutiny of unapproved and counterfeit parts has stayed high since the 2023 forged-release-certificate scandal involving CFM56 parts. The FAA has long-standing guidance on detecting and reporting suspected unapproved parts (AC 21-29), and lessors and insurers keep tightening audit requirements. Fleet retirements of older regional aircraft in 2025-2026 are creating unusually large scrap volumes. Cheap phone-based photo and OCR capture removes the need for special hardware.
revenue_model: Fee per destruction event or per kilogram ($X per event plus a metal revenue share, typically netting near zero out of pocket for the airline). Annual chain-of-custody programs for lessors and MROs. Later, sell certified segregated alloy lots to aerospace melters at a premium.
non_obvious_insight: Airlines treat scrap as a solved cost center. Techs know it is the weakest link in traceability. The buyer's pain is not the cost of scrap, it is being named in the paper trail of a counterfeit. Whoever owns certified destruction owns a record that every auditor, lessor and regulator increasingly wants. The metal value pays for the service, so the airline's out-of-pocket is close to zero, and that removes the budget objection.
first_30_days: Choose one metro with a regional hub plus several 145 shops. Buy a used band saw or plasma cutter and a tag punch, and line up a metals dealer that will accept segregated alloys. Have an aviation attorney draft a certificate of destruction that cites the operator's own manual procedure and AC 21-29. Offer the first scrap-cage clear-out free to 3-5 quality managers, with before and after photos and a metal check. Ask two lessor technical reps for introductions, since they carry the bigger volume.
